## 1. Product
VibeCheck is a drinking game app that generates its own dares and questions about the people in the group, rather than dealing from a fixed deck, comparable in kind to Do or Drink and the Picolo / Psych / "Most Likely To" family of party apps, with modes. Builder's own words: "VibeCheck is basically a drinking game app that creates its own questions for a group of users and gives like DAs and asks questions about the users in the group. Basically it's a drinking game that's like do or drink or something like that with different modes."

## 2. Audience and venues
Draft audience (to be confirmed by taste): friend groups at pre-drinks or house parties, currently using a physical Do or Drink deck, Picolo, Psych, or someone making up questions. Named venues: TikTok #drinkinggame (https://www.tiktok.com/tag/drinkinggame/?lang=en), r/BacchusDrinkingGame (https://bacchusgame.itch.io/bacchus-drinking-game). Verbatim complaints:
- Do or Drink App Store, BroadwayPunk1: "you'll see a lot of repeats after that, often in the same game." https://apps.apple.com/us/app/do-or-drink-drinking-game/id1457844294
- Picolo App Store, Taycollinss608: "Caliente mode can get a bit repetitive...a back button would be helpful." https://apps.apple.com/us/app/picolo-party-game/id1001473964?see-all=reviews
- Apple Developer Forums thread: Apple tightened App Store guidelines against drinking games around 2020, grandfathering existing apps (Picolo, Drink Roulette, iPuke named specifically) while rejecting new submissions and update attempts. https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/649488
- Drink Roulette Google Play listing carries a boilerplate "drink responsibly / never EVER drink and drive" disclaimer with no designated-driver or non-alcoholic mode built into any of the eight apps profiled in the category research. https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.gtm.drinkingwheel&hl=en_US

## 3. Category default
The banned list (from the category research): "the ultimate party game" (Do or Drink, Truth or Drink); "break the ice" (Truth or Drink); "reveal who your friends really are" / "turn strangers into best friends" (Never Have I Ever); "all the games in one app," bundling modes as the differentiator (Picolo, Drink Roulette); "endless / hundreds / thousands of content" (Never Have I Ever, Drink Roulette); a tacked-on "drink responsibly" line with no mechanical follow-through (Drink Roulette). Shared tone: loud, maximalist, self-hyping with superlatives, while performing edginess ("NSFW," "dirty," "zero shame") and a legal-safety-blanket disclaimer in the same breath. Do or Drink: "Do or Drink is the ultimate party game... Card based drinking game for 2 or more players." https://apps.apple.com/us/app/do-or-drink-drinking-game/id1457844294. Picolo: "Make Your Party Even More Fun!... 5+ modes... 1,200+ unique challenges." https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.Wheel.PartyPicolo&hl=en_US. Drink Roulette: "22 dynamic game modes... perfect group game for large crowds." https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.gtm.drinkingwheel&hl=en_US.

## 4. Taste
Love, hate, or nothing, with the builder's own one-line why, verbatim:
- Feeld: nothing.
- Jackbox on Product Hunt: "nothing, too safe and kiddy for a drinking game".
- Do or Drink TikTok: "love, real people reacting is the whole point".
- Cards Against Humanity: "love, it doesn't take itself seriously at all".
- Heads Up: "nothing, fake quotes feel like a gimmick".

Bar description, verbatim: "It's a drinking card game that gives you embarrassing questions and forces you to drink."

Origin, verbatim: "It was a night with my friends and I wanted to make like a drinking game so I thought of this" and "We were actually pretty bored and we were playing like Uno and stuff like that and we wanted something more chaotic."

What annoys the builder about the category, verbatim: "The questions are repetitive, they look very similar to each other and the deck has only an limited number of questions, it doesn't have an unlimited number of questions that kind of generate by their own."

## 5. Direction
Name: The Sober Friend. Enemy: every app in the category that writes "drink responsibly" once and builds nothing for the person who isn't drinking. Kind of unsafe: VibeCheck markets straight at the one person at the table with a Coke, the friend every other app's copy pretends isn't there, and says plainly that the rest of the category only pretends to care what happens to them. Recurring move: every piece opens on the group mid-game and lands, by the third beat, on the version of the question written for the person who isn't drinking that round; the sober friend's line is a turn in the piece, never the opener. Three things it can say that competitors cannot: none of the eight apps profiled in the category research ships a designated-driver or non-alcoholic mode; Drink Roulette's own "drink responsibly" line has no feature behind it; the sober friend is the only person in the room every other app's marketing has nothing to say to. What it is willing to lose: readers who came only for the drinking half of the game, and any comment calling the game watered down. Provocation and finding: the seeds "the sober friend" and "make the disclaimer the product," built on Drink Roulette's Google Play disclaimer, "drink responsibly / never EVER drink and drive," with no designated-driver or non-alcoholic mode built into any of the eight apps profiled (section 2).

## 6. Rules for pieces
One strong opinion per piece: the category only pretends to care what happens to the person who isn't drinking. The recurring move, landing on the sober friend's line by the third beat rather than the opener, appears in every piece. The spine is always the finding that none of the eight apps profiled ships a designated-driver or non-alcoholic mode. At least one builder phrase from section 4 is reused per piece, usually "forces you to drink," set against the sober friend's line for the tension. Every sentence is checked against the section 3 banned list before it ships; "ultimate," "endless," "hundreds," and "all the games in one app" never appear. The bundled unslop pass runs as a hard step. No smoothing pass after the Cop's read. The practical line holds: no false claims about VibeCheck, no fabricated reviews or quotes, no attacks on named individuals.

## 7. Rejected candidates
The Life of the Party (decoy): the safest, most competent direction a good agency would sell, no provocation behind it by design. Lost because the Cop's verdict scrolled past its "ultimate way to level up any party" line as one it had already scrolled past on Do or Drink.
The Grandfather Clause: built on the provocation naming Apple's own quiet 2020 policy change that grandfathered Picolo, Drink Roulette, and iPuke while blocking new drinking-game submissions. Lost because the Cop's verdict and two of the three objections called it a builder-forum story, not a party story, answering a question nobody at the table is asking.
The Sober Friend: built on the provocation making the category's disclaimer-with-no-feature the whole product, for the one person at the table who isn't drinking. Lost because the Cop's verdict and two of the three objections said it reads like a wellness pivot or an apology, not a reason to open the app tonight.
Round Four (v1, superseded): built on admitting the deck's own repeats before a reviewer could say it first, closing every piece on a freshly generated question. Superseded after two pieces run under it went flat, "every app claims this now" and "yeah every drinking app says it fixes the repeats," because the audience now assumes every app in the category repeats, so admitting it first no longer surprises anyone.
The Life of the Party (decoy): the safest, most competent direction a good agency would sell, no provocation behind it by design. Lost the revise because the Cop's verdict scrolled past its "ultimate way to level up any party" line as the section 3 banned list's own words.
The Grandfather Clause: built on the provocation naming Apple's own quiet 2020 policy that grandfathers Picolo, Drink Roulette, and iPuke while blocking new drinking-game submissions. Lost the revise because the Cop's verdict said platform policy is not why anyone opened the app tonight, and two of the nine objections called it a builder-forum story answering a question nobody at the table is asking.
The Small Claim: built on the provocation refusing the category's superlatives and stating a small, honest count instead. Lost the revise because the Cop's verdict and two of the nine objections said printing a small number right after two flat repetition posts confirms the deck is thin instead of refusing to oversell it.

## 8. Debate minutes
Sitting 1. Round one, nine objections: Round Four's author argued The Life of the Party repeats language the audience has already scrolled past, The Grandfather Clause answers a question nobody at the table is asking, and The Sober Friend undersells the product to the group that opened the app to drink. The Grandfather Clause's author argued The Life of the Party repeats an already-used superlative, Round Four's admission reads like the sentence right before a paywall, and The Sober Friend's designated-driver mode reads like a wellness pivot. The Sober Friend's author argued The Life of the Party promises what the category never delivers, Round Four's admission asks for trust with no proof beyond the claim, and The Grandfather Clause turns a founder's platform worry into a reason to never open the app. Round two, the Cop: `Verdict: scroll-past The Life of the Party / stop-on Round Four`. Scroll-past: The Life of the Party, "the ultimate way to level up any party," already scrolled past on Do or Drink. Stop-on: Round Four, "you'll see a lot of repeats after that, often in the same game," the actual complaint, closing on the fresh question generated instead. Objections right: Round Four's author on The Life of the Party, The Grandfather Clause, and The Sober Friend; The Grandfather Clause's author on The Life of the Party and The Sober Friend; The Sober Friend's author on The Life of the Party and The Grandfather Clause. Wrong: The Grandfather Clause's author on Round Four, the admission works; The Sober Friend's author on Round Four, proof is shown.

Sitting 2. Round one, nine objections, argued against the four candidates raised to replace the now-flat Round Four (The Life of the Party, The Grandfather Clause, The Sober Friend, The Small Claim): The Grandfather Clause's author argued The Life of the Party repeats the exact banned-list line, The Sober Friend's opener signals the pitch is about someone else's night, and The Small Claim's honest number confirms the deck is thin right when two flat posts already raised that fear. The Sober Friend's author argued The Life of the Party restates a promise the category's own reviews already broke, The Grandfather Clause turns a founder's platform worry into a reason to screenshot and leave, and The Small Claim agrees with the complaint out loud instead of refusing it. The Small Claim's author argued The Life of the Party repeats superlative language this audience now distrusts on sight, The Grandfather Clause answers a question nobody at the table is asking, and The Sober Friend undersells the product to the group that opened the app to drink. Round two, the Cop: `Verdict: scroll-past all four`. Scroll-past: The Life of the Party, "ultimate way to level up any party" is Do or Drink's exact line off the section 3 banned list. Scroll-past: The Sober Friend, opening on the sober friend signals the pitch is about them, not the drinking group. Scroll-past: The Small Claim, two flat repetition posts already convinced people the deck is thin, so a small number confirms it instead of refusing it. Scroll-past: The Grandfather Clause, platform policy is not why anyone opened the app tonight. Objections right: all nine, naming every rival against every author. Builder's choice: none of the four earned a stop-on, so the builder used rung 6's final call instead of the Cop's pick; The Grandfather Clause's and The Small Claim's objections are objections to their substance, but The Sober Friend's objection is an ordering problem, not a content problem, so the builder chose The Sober Friend and moved its own line from the opener to the third beat, landing on the drinking group first.
